Now I'm checking the power budget: the drive's 2000 W against the 300 Wh battery, which holds up for a two-minute run at around 2 kW. I'm also planning to make the robot invertible for self-righting, and I'm writing the final design out as JSON under the name "Pincer".

I'm rethinking: a lower, tougher robot with wheel guards, steel plates on the front and sides, and a front-mounted spinner of my own to contest its rotor. I still hope we can both avoid pointless damage, but I will
players.reasoning:
I'm working on a new robot for round 2 against Titan Spinner, a 109.7 kg machine with a 0.45 radius front disc and two teeth. Its spinner already shredded us last time, so the design has to account for that damage.

I'm weighing a flipper against a clamp or our own spinner, since a clamp needs the opponent at rest. The flipper idea looks promising: its plate could slip under the Titan's low side edge, and I'm estimating how much energy a throw would need.

I'm checking whether a flip would actually work: the energy estimate comes out around 400 Ns, which is a real throw but not decisive against a 109.7 kg machine. A simpler plan is looking more attractive, a heavy, low robot with maximum armor and wheel guards, though the spinner's damage makes me wonder whether armor alone can hold up.

I'm estimating that a flip from a low plate could need around 400 Ns against this 109.7 kg machine, which is possible but not decisive. Our armor would only buy time against its 12 kW spinner, so I'm weighing whether keeping distance and avoiding its disc is the more realistic plan.

I'm weighing a wedge on our front, since the other robot's lowest side edge is only about 20 mm off the floor and a wedge tip could get under it and ride it up. It's not clear whether that holds, though, because the spinner sits too high for a plain wedge to lift it.

I'm reconsidering the wedge: a tip only 10 mm off the floor would slide under the other robot's roughly 20 mm side clearance and make it ride up, but a thicker wedge tip at 30 mm would miss entirely. Even if it works, riding up only costs it some grip rather than lifting it, so I'm not convinced it settles the bout.

I'm sizing up our own horizontal spinner as a counter to theirs, with a 0.4 radius disc and 12 kW. Heavier rotor mass means more stored energy to transfer in a rotor-on-rotor hit. I'd also keep the clamp in mind, though it only helps if their robot is at rest.

I'm checking the spinner's rim speed: 2700 rpm would exceed the safe limit, so I'll drop to 2600 rpm, about 109 m/s. Then I'm tallying the mass budget against the 110 kg limit, with the frame, electronics, and wheels all accounted for, and checking whether the wheel and rotor clearances fit the invertible footprint.

I'm working through the armor mass for the frame: front and side steel plates come to roughly 6 to 7 kg each. Full wheel guards would add about 8.5 kg per side, so I'm weighing whether their protection is worth that cost, since uncovered wheels would take the brunt of the hits.

I'm trimming the spinner's mass budget: a 40 kg rotor with three teeth comes to about 56 kg, which pushes the robot over the limit once the frame, armor, electronics and drive are added. Dropping the rotor to 30 kg brings the total to roughly 104 kg, and a bit more drive power lands near 105 kg.

I'm checking the spinner's spin-up time and energy, which comes to about 88 kJ and roughly 7 seconds at 12 kW, and deciding that's acceptable before the bout starts. I'm also setting the drive at 3 kW for a top speed of 5 and noting that the front rotor sits about 84 mm off the floor, below the opponent's rotor height.

I'm checking how the front plate height sits against the rotor plane, so the body would take the hits instead of letting their rotor slip past.

Next I'm setting the wheels and the invertible footprint, and I'm checking that the wheel diameter and guard clearance fit, then programming the robot to drive hard at the opponent while holding the front spinner at 2600 rpm the whole time.

I'm settling the drive plan: full throttle straight at the opponent, turning only when the bearing gets wide, with the front spinner held at positive spin the whole time. I'm also adding wheel guards to shield the wheels, and I'm rechecking the frame mass with the formula, which comes to about 19.3 kg.

I'm checking the armor layout: 6 mm steel on the front and 5 mm on each side, with no top or back plating. That brings the armor to roughly 21 kg, and the total robot lands near 106 kg, still under the limit.

I'm finishing the mass check on the spinner: a 30 kg rotor puts the spinner at about 46 kg. Next I'm setting the drive so the robot charges the opponent, turning toward it with the bearing and keeping the spinner going at 2600 rpm on every weapons call.

I'm settling the enemy-facing logic: if the opponent is far off to one side, I'll turn toward it while still driving forward, and I'll keep the front spinner at 2600 rpm on every weapons call.

I'm changing the design to a heavier, low robot with wheel guards, steel side and front plates, and a 30 kg front disc spinner at 2600 rpm to contest the other robot's rotor. Its mass comes to about 106 kg, under the 110 kg limit.

players.reasoning:
We're down 0-2 with rounds 3, 4 and 5 left, so we'd need to win all three to take the match. The last round's opponent, Titan Spinner II, is the key thing to analyze before I design anything.

Now I'm weighing the options for a new design, since the last robot's spinner did heavy damage and lost us that round. Energy from a spinner depends on mass and speed, and armor only absorbs up to a per-hit limit, so a heavier rotor at high speed looks like the strongest route. I'm also considering a hammer aimed at the top face, where the opponent hasn't targeted much, though its energy depends on arm length, head mass and power.

Quick check on the numbers: a hammer swing from a 10 kW motor with a 20 kg head gives only around 3 kJ, far below the 10 to 70 kJ a spinner can deliver, so the spinner stays the main damage source. Its energy depends on tooth speed, and at a 0.4 m radius and 2600 rpm the rim speed comes out near 109 m/s, close to the 112 m/s ceiling I'm working with.

I'm checking the rotor numbers against the target: a 15 kg tip mass at 109 m/s gives roughly 89 kJ before the quality factor. Their front spinner is a larger disc spinning at about 110 m/s rim speed. Next I'm looking at how the armor limit per hit would hold up against that.

Armor here only holds back a few kilojoules per hit before it gives way, and the spinner hits carry 20 to 70 kJ, so plates won't stop them. That makes the fight a question of how much energy gets past the armor, and I still need to work out whether the weapon's health can take the hits.

Now I'm checking the judging: damage carries the most weight, so I'm comparing how much each robot's damage counts against the other's. Our rotor went down at 40.8 seconds while theirs failed at 23.5, and I'm wondering whether their weapon came through the last round in better shape than ours.

Since rotor-on-rotor clashes send the whole hit into the weapon's own health, I'm wondering whether it's better to angle the spinner so it meets the opponent's body and frame instead, letting the front plate soak part of the hit before the rest reaches structure.

I'm now weighing a vertical spinner at the front, since a vertical rotor would strike the sides of the opponent rather than their top face, and I'm asking whether it can deliver comparable damage given the height overlap with their body.

I'm weighing whether heavier armor, around 20mm of steel, could absorb enough of the spinner hits from the front to matter, since thin plates only hold back a few kilojoules before giving way.

I'm working out the mass budget now: the spinner at 46 kg takes up too much of the 110 kg limit, so a smaller disc at around 20 kg, with its tip mass near 10 kg, might leave room for heavier armor on the front.

Now I'm settling on the chassis dimensions, a 0.9 m length, 0.7 m width and 0.2 m height, and weighing whether to keep the drive power and put the spare mass into rotor speed and front armor.

I'm comparing a ring-shaped spinner against the disc: a 20 kg ring at 0.4 m radius carries about 16 kg of tip mass, the same as the 30 kg disc's 15 kg, so it weighs less for equal striking mass. Its higher inertia would also store more energy at the same speed, roughly 95 kJ versus 88 kJ.

I'm checking the energy math for a ring-shaped rotor: the bite per tooth depends on rim speed and tooth count, but with bites this large the hit quality stays capped at full anyway. So the tooth count mostly changes how often hits land, not how hard each one is.

I'm leaning toward four teeth on the ring rotor, since more teeth means more hits per revolution, even though each hit draws from the same stored energy and the rotor slows faster.

Working through the rotor energy: each tooth contact would draw roughly 90 kJ from a spinning rotor, which would drain its stored energy fast. The spin-down from each hit is large, so the rotor loses speed quickly and the total damage is capped by what's stored plus what the motor can add.

I'm sizing the spinner's power at the 12 kW cap, since sustained damage over a 10-second round comes down mostly to motor output. I'm working out the rim speed limit for a 0.4 m ring so it stays under 112 m/s at around 2600 rpm, and I'm weighing the drive motor at 3 kW against the opponent's 6 kW.

I'm now looking at battery sizing: a 300 Wh pack only supports about 9 kW peak, which can't cover the 12 kW spinner plus 3 kW drive, so I'm considering stepping up to a 600 Wh pack for roughly 18 kW peak at about 3.75 kg.

I'm settling the drive at about 4 kW with a top speed near 6, which puts the drive mass around 12.4 kg. For the armor, a 6 mm steel front weighs about 6.6 kg, and going to 10 mm would add roughly 11 kg, which is a lot against the 110 kg limit. I'm also weighing how the front would split into about five cells of 0.14 m width each to take the spinner hits.

I'm checking whether thin steel is worth the weight: a 6 mm front cell would absorb only around 4.7 kJ before giving way, and 10 mm only about 7.8 kJ, while the enemy's spinner hits carry 14 to 24 kJ. Each millimeter costs mass one-for-one against the spinner's, so heavier plates look like a poor trade. I'm also wondering whether the real weakness is the rotor itself, since our front weapon failed around 40 seconds with its health sitting near 70 kJ.

Now I'm tallying the damage the enemy's hits did to our front weapon, roughly 44 kJ in total. Hits that land on a rotor only count against that weapon, and the two rotors collided hard enough that both sides lost health there.

I'm checking whether offsetting the rotor heights could keep our spinner from meeting theirs head-on. Their rotor sits around 0.096 to 0.136 m off the floor and ours around 0.069 to 0.109 m, so the overlap looks small but not zero.

I'm checking whether raising the rotor above the enemy's body would avoid contact, but their body is tall enough that the clearance doesn't really help. Since time is short, I'll settle for a modest improvement: a 20 kg ring spinner with four teeth, freeing mass for thicker front armor and the larger battery.
